encounters.cc: One week of poor feeding, high-pitched crying, and difficulty focusing eyes.

lines: One week of poor feeding, high-pitched crying, and difficulty focusing eyes.
The infant with VHL, hydrocephalus, congenital toxoplasmosis, and laryngomalacia presents following Otolaryngology evaluation today.
The mother reports the infant has been irritable and seems to have difficulty focusing his eyes, denying fever, vomiting, or diarrhea.
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence
The mother had a normal pregnancy but recalls having a "flu-like illness" during her first trimester for which she did not seek medical attention.
- Non-sterile umbilical cord ligation at unassisted home birth
- Maternal first-trimester toxoplasmosis infection (untreated flu-like illness)
- Suspected autosomal dominant Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
- No history of sickle cell disease or cystic fibrosis
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: None (infant).
On examination, the infant has a head circumference in the 98th percentile, a bulging anterior fontanelle, and bilateral diffuse chorioretinal scars on fundoscopic examination.
The infant also exhibits generalized hypotonia.
A CT scan of the head shows hydrocephalus.

encounters.cc: Poor feeding, lethargy, and high-pitched cry progressing to difficulty awakening.

lines: Poor feeding, lethargy, and high-pitched cry progressing to difficulty awakening.
The infant presents with worsening symptoms evaluated earlier today for laryngomalacia and toxoplasmosis, with known Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, hydrocephalus with VP shunt, and chorioretinitis.
The parents also report that the infant's cry has become high-pitched and that he has been more difficult to awaken over the past few days.
The infant was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery.
His birth weight was 3.5 kg, and he was exclusively breastfed.
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence
- Non-sterile umbilical cord ligation at unassisted home birth
- Maternal first-trimester toxoplasmosis infection (untreated flu-like illness)
- Suspected autosomal dominant Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
- No history of sickle cell disease or cystic fibrosis
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: None (infant).
Vital signs are within normal limits.
On physical examination, the infant is jaundiced and has a poor suck reflex.
His muscle tone is increased, and he exhibits intermittent back arching.
The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable.

encounters.cc: Progressively worsening body stiffness, poor feeding, and difficulty opening mouth.

lines: Progressively worsening body stiffness, poor feeding, and difficulty opening mouth.

The patient is a male infant with Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence, congenital toxoplasmosis with chorioretinitis on pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid therapy, and laryngomalacia who presents to the emergency department approximately one month following his prior neonatology admission for acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
He was born at home via an unassisted vaginal delivery without complications.
His umbilical cord was cut using a kitchen knife that had not been sterilized and was tied with household twine.
The parents have not brought him to a healthcare facility since birth, and the infant has not received any vaccinations.
Over the past 48 hours, he has become increasingly irritable, with episodes of generalized stiffness and arching of his back when touched or stimulated.
His mother also reports that he has stopped breastfeeding and frequently clenches his jaw shut.
- Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy (Bilirubin-Induced Neurologic Dysfunction) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence
- Non-sterile umbilical cord ligation at unassisted home birth
- Maternal first-trimester toxoplasmosis infection (untreated flu-like illness)
- Suspected autosomal dominant Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
- No history of sickle cell disease or cystic fibrosis
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: None (infant).
On examination, the infant has diffuse hypertonia, clenched fists, a rigid jaw, and opisthotonus (severe arching of the back and neck).
Mild umbilical erythema is noted without pus or foul odor.

encounters.cc: Two-day history of fever, irritability, and poor feeding in a 6-week-old infant.

lines: Two-day history of fever, irritability, and poor feeding in a 6-week-old infant.

This 6-week-old male infant with Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence, congenital toxoplasmosis, and recent recovery from neonatal tetanus is brought to the emergency department by his parents due to a 2-day history of fever and irritability.
The mother reports that the infant has been feeding poorly and has decreased activity.
- Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy (Bilirubin-Induced Neurologic Dysfunction) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence
The infant was born at term via vaginal delivery without complications and the mother's prenatal screening was unremarkable.
- Non-sterile umbilical cord ligation at unassisted home birth
- Maternal first-trimester toxoplasmosis infection (untreated flu-like illness)
- Suspected autosomal dominant Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
- No history of sickle cell disease or cystic fibrosis
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: None (infant).
Temperature of 38.9°C (102°F), heart rate of 160/min, and respiratory rate of 40/min
On examination, the infant is lethargic and has a temperature of 38.9°C (102°F), heart rate of 160/min, and respiratory rate of 40/min.
Lumbar puncture reveals cloudy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with the following results: WBC: 2,200/mm³ (80% neutrophils), RBC: 50/mm³, Protein: 150 mg/dL, Glucose: 20 mg/dL (serum glucose 90 mg/dL).
A full septic workup is initiated.

encounters.cc: Five-day history of paroxysmal coughing with whooping sound and post-cough cyanosis.

lines: Five-day history of paroxysmal coughing with whooping sound and post-cough cyanosis.

The patient is a male with Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence, congenital toxoplasmosis on chronic antimicrobial therapy, and prior laryngomalacia and recovered neonatal tetanus who presents with a five-day history of paroxysmal coughing.
His mother reports that during these episodes, he becomes red-faced and struggles to catch his breath.
She has also noticed a "whooping" sound when he inhales afterward.
He has not had any fever, vomiting, or nasal congestion.
- Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy (Bilirubin-Induced Neurologic Dysfunction) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Late-onset neonatal sepsis with Group B Streptococcal meningitis (diagnosed 2020-03-15)
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence
He was born at term and has not yet received any vaccinations.
- Non-sterile umbilical cord ligation at unassisted home birth
His older sibling recently had a prolonged cough but was never formally diagnosed.
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: None (infant).
Afebrile with oxygen saturation of 97% on room air
He appears mildly distressed but is alert and feeding adequately between coughing fits.
Nasopharyngeal swab for PCR is pending.

His parents report irritability, vomiting more frequently over the past two weeks, and difficulty looking upward.

- Late-onset neonatal sepsis with Group B Streptococcal meningitis (diagnosed 2020-03-15)
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence

- No history of sickle cell disease or cystic fibrosis

On physical examination, the infant has a head circumference in the 99th percentile, a bulging fontanelle, and "sunset" eyes.

encounters.cc: Two days of irritability, high-pitched crying, forceful vomiting, and excessive sleepiness.

lines: Two days of irritability, high-pitched crying, forceful vomiting, and excessive sleepiness.
This 3-year-old male with congenital hydrocephalus and ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence returns with new symptoms.
His mother reports that he has been vomiting forcefully after feedings and seems more sleepy than usual.
The child's immunizations are up to date, and there is no history of recent illness or trauma.
- Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with acute bilirubin encephalopathy (Bilirubin-Induced Neurologic Dysfunction) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Late-onset neonatal sepsis with Group B Streptococcal meningitis (diagnosed 2020-03-15)
- Congenital hydrocephalus with ventriculoperitoneal shunt dependence
The child was born at term without complications and has met all developmental milestones.
- Non-sterile umbilical cord ligation at unassisted home birth
- Maternal first-trimester toxoplasmosis infection (untreated flu-like illness)
- Suspected autosomal dominant Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
- No history of sickle cell disease or cystic fibrosis
Smoking: Never. Alcohol: None. Occupation: None (infant).
His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 142/min, and respirations are 38/min.
On examination, the infant is lethargic but arousable.
The anterior fontanelle is full and tense.
Cranial nerves are intact, and fundoscopic examination reveals bilateral papilledema.
There is no neck stiffness, and the remainder of the neurological examination is nonfocal.
A head ultrasound shows dilated lateral ventricles.
